CHAPTER E2.3 · ELECTIVE 2

CHAPTER E2.3 · ELECTIVE 2 · FEBRUARY

Population models

Eggs become larvae, larvae become beetles, and beetles lay eggs again. How many beetles will there be in three, in ten, in a hundred generations? Customers switch back and forth between electricity providers every year. How will they be distributed in the long run? Both questions are answered by a transition matrix: its powers show the future, the limit matrix and the fixed vector the state that everything is heading for.

8 LESSONS3 UNITSELECTIVE 2
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • describe transitions between states with a transition graph and a transition matrix
  • calculate developments with powers of matrices, forwards and backwards
  • recognise and explain cyclic behaviour, growth and extinction of a population
  • find the limit matrix and the fixed vector and interpret them as the long-term distribution

UNIT 13 LESSONS

1Transition matrices and powers

After one time step there are $8 \cdot 50 = 400$ eggs, $0.25 \cdot 800 = 200$ larvae and $0.5 \cdot 200 = 100$ beetles. Every new number is a sum of proportions of the old ones: exactly one row of a matrix times the column vector of the old numbers.

The state at time $n$ is a vector $\vec{x}_n$. The transition matrix $U$ contains in column $j$ what one individual of state $j$ becomes in the next step: column means “from”, row means “to”. The transition graph shows the same as arrows. Because every step is the same multiplication again, the whole future lies in the powers of $U$.

KEY POINT · TRANSITION MATRIX

$\vec{x}_{n+1} = U \cdot \vec{x}_n$   and so   $\vec{x}_n = U^n \cdot \vec{x}_0$. The entry $u_{ij}$ is the proportion (or the number) with which state $j$ contributes to state $i$.

Backwards: if $U$ is invertible, then $\vec{x}_{n-1} = U^{-1} \cdot \vec{x}_n$.

Beetle model: $U = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & f \\ a & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & b & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ with the survival proportions $a$ (egg → larva), $b$ (larva → beetle) and the number $f$ of eggs per beetle.

Leslie matrix: population matrices of this kind were studied by the British ecologist Patrick Leslie in 1945. Source: P. H. Leslie, On the use of matrices in certain population mathematics, Biometrika 33 (1945).

On the CAS you calculate $U^{10}$ directly as a power, without multiplying ten times.

INTERACTIVE · BEETLES AND CUSTOMERS

Go step by step and watch the three curves. Change the number $f$ of eggs per beetle: for which $f$ does everything repeat, when does the population grow, when does it die out? Customers switching comes in unit 3.

EXAMPLE 1 · THREE STEPS

Calculate $\vec{x}_1$, $\vec{x}_2$, $\vec{x}_3$ for $U = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 8 \\ 0.25 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.5 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\vec{x}_0 = \begin{pmatrix} 800 \\ 200 \\ 50 \end{pmatrix}$.

$\vec{x}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 400 \\ 200 \\ 100 \end{pmatrix}$, $\vec{x}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 800 \\ 100 \\ 100 \end{pmatrix}$, $\vec{x}_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 800 \\ 200 \\ 50 \end{pmatrix}$.

After three steps everything is as at the start.

EXAMPLE 2 · POWERS

Calculate $U^2$ and $U^3$. Use them to explain example 1.

$U^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 0.125 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, $U^3 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = I$.

$\vec{x}_3 = U^3 \cdot \vec{x}_0 = I \cdot \vec{x}_0 = \vec{x}_0$. For every starting vector the development repeats with period 3.

EXERCISES

Draw the transition graph for $U = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 6 \\ 0.5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.4 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and interpret the three numbers.

Egg → larva 0.5 (half of the eggs survive), larva → beetle 0.4 (40% of the larvae become beetles), beetle → egg 6 (every beetle lays 6 eggs).

For this matrix calculate $\vec{x}_1$ and $\vec{x}_2$ with $\vec{x}_0 = \begin{pmatrix} 600 \\ 100 \\ 50 \end{pmatrix}$.

$\vec{x}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 300 \\ 300 \\ 40 \end{pmatrix}$, $\vec{x}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 240 \\ 150 \\ 120 \end{pmatrix}$

In the beetle model with $f = 8$ (example 1) there are 400 eggs, 200 larvae and 100 beetles today. What did the population look like one step earlier? Explain why $U^{-1} = U^2$ here.

From $U^3 = I$ it follows that $U \cdot U^2 = I$, so $U^{-1} = U^2$. $\vec{x}_{-1} = U^2 \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 400 \\ 200 \\ 100 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 800 \\ 200 \\ 50 \end{pmatrix}$, exactly $\vec{x}_0$ from example 1.

An animal species has three age classes: young, yearlings, adults. 50% of the young become yearlings, 70% of the yearlings become adults, 80% of the adults survive every year and stay adults. Yearlings have 1 young on average, adults 2. Set up $U$.

Columns “from” young, yearling, adult; rows “to”: $U = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0.5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.7 & 0.8 \end{pmatrix}$. The 0.8 on the diagonal: adults stay adults.

Use the CAS to calculate $\vec{x}_{10}$ and $\vec{x}_{11}$ for the model from the last exercise and $\vec{x}_0 = \begin{pmatrix} 100 \\ 50 \\ 50 \end{pmatrix}$. By what factor does the population eventually grow per year? Compare the proportions of the age classes.

$\vec{x}_{10} \approx \begin{pmatrix} 2066 \\ 771 \\ 999 \end{pmatrix}$, $\vec{x}_{11} \approx \begin{pmatrix} 2769 \\ 1033 \\ 1339 \end{pmatrix}$ (rounded). Every class and the total grow from year to year by the same factor, about 1.34. The proportions stay almost the same: about 54% young, 20% yearlings, 26% adults. Unlike the beetle, there is no cycle, because the adults live for several years.

UNIT 22 LESSONS

2Cycles, growth and extinction

In the beetle model, after three steps one egg becomes $a \cdot b \cdot f$ eggs again: first a larva with proportion $a$, then a beetle with proportion $b$, then $f$ eggs. With $a = 0.25$, $b = 0.5$, $f = 8$ that is exactly 1.

The same holds for every class. That is why $U^3 = a\,b\,f \cdot I$: after three steps every class has been multiplied by the factor $q = a\,b\,f$. Whether the population survives is decided by this factor alone. Between the multiples of 3 the numbers fluctuate, because the classes take their turns one after another.

KEY POINT · LONG-TERM BEHAVIOUR IN THE BEETLE MODEL

$U^3 = q \cdot I$ with $q = a \cdot b \cdot f$, so $\vec{x}_{3k} = q^k \cdot \vec{x}_0$.

$q = 1$: cyclic with period 3 · $q > 1$: growth · $q < 1$: extinction in the long run.

In general you read off the long-term behaviour from the powers $U^n$, for large $n$ with the CAS.

Kept stable: to keep a population constant when $q > 1$, you have to remove a fixed proportion in every cycle, for example by pest control.

EXAMPLE 3 · TEN EGGS PER BEETLE

How does the population from example 1 develop if every beetle lays 10 eggs?

$q = 0.25 \cdot 0.5 \cdot 10 = 1.25$, so $U^3 = 1.25 \cdot I$ and $\vec{x}_3 = 1.25 \cdot \vec{x}_0 = \begin{pmatrix} 1000 \\ 250 \\ 62.5 \end{pmatrix}$.

Every three steps each class grows by 25%.

EXAMPLE 4 · HOW MANY EGGS ARE NEEDED?

Because of a pesticide only 20% of the larvae survive. How many eggs must a beetle lay so that the population does not die out?

$q = 0.25 \cdot 0.2 \cdot f \ge 1 \iff f \ge 20$. At least 20 eggs per beetle.

EXERCISES

Decide for $U = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 6 \\ 0.5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.4 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ whether the population grows, is cyclic or dies out.

$q = 0.5 \cdot 0.4 \cdot 6 = 1.2 > 1$: growth, by 20% every three steps.

For $f = 8$ and $\vec{x}_0 = \begin{pmatrix} 800 \\ 200 \\ 50 \end{pmatrix}$ calculate the number of beetles after 100 steps.

$100 = 3 \cdot 33 + 1$, so $\vec{x}_{100} = U \cdot \vec{x}_0 = \vec{x}_1$: 100 beetles.

For which $b$ is the model with $a = 0.2$ and $f = 25$ cyclic? Then give $U^2$ and $U^{-1}$.

$0.2 \cdot b \cdot 25 = 1 \Rightarrow b = 0.2$. $U^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 \\ 0.04 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = U^{-1}$.

Prove $U^3 = a\,b\,f \cdot I$ for $U = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & f \\ a & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & b & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ by first calculating $U^2$ in general. What follows for $U^{3k+1}$?

$U^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & bf & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & af \\ ab & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, $U^3 = U \cdot U^2 = \begin{pmatrix} abf & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & abf & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & abf \end{pmatrix}$. $\square$ Hence $U^{3k+1} = (abf)^k \cdot U$.

TEST YOURSELF!

$a = 0.25$, $b = 0.5$, $f = 10$: what is $q$?

$0.25 \cdot 0.5 \cdot 10$

$a = 0.25$, $b = 0.2$: minimum number of eggs per beetle so that the population does not die out?

$0.05 f \ge 1$

UNIT 33 LESSONS

3Limit matrix and fixed vector

Municipal utility $S$ and competitor $K$: $P = \begin{pmatrix} 0.9 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.8 \end{pmatrix}$, start $\begin{pmatrix} 600 \\ 400 \end{pmatrix}$. After one year $\begin{pmatrix} 620 \\ 380 \end{pmatrix}$, after two $\begin{pmatrix} 634 \\ 366 \end{pmatrix}$. The municipal utility gains, but more and more slowly. Where does this lead?

When customers move, nobody is lost and nobody is added: every column of $P$ has the sum 1. Such matrices are called stochastic. Their powers $P^n$ often approach a limit matrix $G$ whose columns are all the same. This column vector is the fixed vector $\vec{v}$: a distribution that no longer changes under $P$. You find it without powers from the system of equations $P \cdot \vec{v} = \vec{v}$ with the extra condition that the proportions add up to 1.

KEY POINT · LIMIT MATRIX AND FIXED VECTOR

Fixed vector: $P \cdot \vec{v} = \vec{v} \iff (P - I) \cdot \vec{v} = \vec{0}$, plus $v_1 + v_2 + \ldots = 1$ for a distribution in proportions.

Limit matrix: $G = \lim\limits_{n \to \infty} P^n$, all columns are $\vec{v}$. Then for every start $\vec{x}_0$: $\vec{x}_n \to G \cdot \vec{x}_0 = (\text{total}) \cdot \vec{v}$.

So in the long run the distribution does not depend on the start; only the total is preserved.

Not always: in the cyclic beetle model there is no limit matrix, the powers keep jumping between $U$, $U^2$ and $I$.

On the CAS: calculate $P^{50}$ and round to three places. The columns are then practically the fixed vector.

INTERACTIVE · THREE PROVIDERS

Customers switching between three electricity providers: go 10 steps and more. Watch how the columns of $P^n$ become equal and how the curves settle on the fixed vector.

EXAMPLE 5 · THE FIXED VECTOR

Find the fixed vector and the limit matrix for $P = \begin{pmatrix} 0.9 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.8 \end{pmatrix}$.

$(P - I) \cdot \vec{v} = \vec{0}$: $-0.1 v_1 + 0.2 v_2 = 0$, so $v_1 = 2 v_2$. With $v_1 + v_2 = 1$: $v_2 = \tfrac13$, $v_1 = \tfrac23$.

$\vec{v} = \begin{pmatrix} \tfrac23 \\ \tfrac13 \end{pmatrix}$, $G = \begin{pmatrix} \tfrac23 & \tfrac23 \\ \tfrac13 & \tfrac13 \end{pmatrix}$. In the long run: $G \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 600 \\ 400 \end{pmatrix} \approx \begin{pmatrix} 667 \\ 333 \end{pmatrix}$.

EXAMPLE 6 · POWERS ON THE CAS

Calculate $P^5$ and $P^{20}$ and compare with $G$.

$P^5 \approx \begin{pmatrix} 0.723 & 0.555 \\ 0.277 & 0.445 \end{pmatrix}$, $P^{20} \approx \begin{pmatrix} 0.667 & 0.666 \\ 0.333 & 0.334 \end{pmatrix}$.

After 20 years the columns are practically equal, $P^{20} \approx G$.

EXERCISES

Check whether $P = \begin{pmatrix} 0.8 & 0.1 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.7 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.2 & 0.6 \end{pmatrix}$ is stochastic, and interpret the column for provider C.

Column sums: $0.8 + 0.1 + 0.1 = 1$, $0.1 + 0.7 + 0.2 = 1$, $0.2 + 0.2 + 0.6 = 1$ ✓ Of C's customers, 20% switch to A and 20% to B every year, 60% stay.

Find the fixed vector of this matrix without a CAS and compare with the widget.

Two rows of $(P - I)\,\vec{v} = \vec{0}$ and the sum condition are enough; the third row follows from the others.

$-0.2 v_1 + 0.1 v_2 + 0.2 v_3 = 0$, $0.1 v_1 - 0.3 v_2 + 0.2 v_3 = 0$, $v_1 + v_2 + v_3 = 1$. Solution: $\vec{v} = \begin{pmatrix} \tfrac{8}{19} \\ \tfrac{6}{19} \\ \tfrac{5}{19} \end{pmatrix} \approx \begin{pmatrix} 0.421 \\ 0.316 \\ 0.263 \end{pmatrix}$.

With 10,000 customers: how many does provider A have in the long run? Does it matter whether everyone was with C at the start?

$10{,}000 \cdot \tfrac{8}{19} \approx 4211$. No: the limit matrix has nothing but equal columns, so every start with 10,000 customers leads to the same distribution.

Prove: if $P$ is stochastic (all column sums 1), then $P \cdot \vec{x}$ has the same sum of components as $\vec{x}$. Why does this make sense for customers switching, but not for the beetle model?

$\sum_i (P\vec{x})_i = \sum_i \sum_j p_{ij} x_j = \sum_j x_j \sum_i p_{ij} = \sum_j x_j \cdot 1$. $\square$

Customers only switch, they do not disappear. Beetles die and lay eggs: the column sums of the beetle matrix are $a$, $b$ and $f$, not 1, and the total changes.

TEST YOURSELF!

Municipal utility: start 600 and 400. How many customers does the municipal utility have after two years?

$0.9 \cdot 620 + 0.2 \cdot 380$

Second component of the fixed vector of $\begin{pmatrix} 0.9 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.8 \end{pmatrix}$?

$v_1 = 2v_2$, $v_1 + v_2 = 1$

The columns of the limit matrix are …

Every start leads to the same distribution.

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A hire car is returned in Dresden or Leipzig. Of the cars hired in Dresden, 70% come back to Dresden; of those hired in Leipzig, 60% come back to Leipzig. Set up $P$ and find the long-term distribution of the cars.

$P = \begin{pmatrix} 0.7 & 0.4 \\ 0.3 & 0.6 \end{pmatrix}$. $-0.3 v_1 + 0.4 v_2 = 0$, $v_1 + v_2 = 1$: $\vec{v} = \begin{pmatrix} \tfrac47 \\ \tfrac37 \end{pmatrix}$, so just over 57% in Dresden.

Connecting with chapter E2.1: why does the equation $(P - I)\,\vec{v} = \vec{0}$ always have infinitely many solutions for a stochastic matrix, so that you need the sum condition?

The column sums of $P - I$ are all $1 - 1 = 0$: the sum of all rows is the zero row, one row depends on the others. $P - I$ is not invertible, and together with $\vec{v}$ every multiple $r\vec{v}$ is a solution.

Connecting with Year 12: a game of chance has two states, “in the game” and “out”. Each round you stay in the game with probability 0.8; once out, you stay out. Set up $P$. What is the probability of still being in the game after 5 rounds? What is the limit matrix?

$P = \begin{pmatrix} 0.8 & 0 \\ 0.2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. After 5 rounds: $0.8^5 \approx 0.328$. $P^n \to G = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$: in the long run everyone drops out, “out” is an absorbing state.

Open problem: invent a $2 \times 2$ transition matrix whose powers have no limit matrix. What happens to a distribution then?

For example $P = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$: everyone switches every year. $P^2 = I$, the powers jump between $P$ and $I$. A distribution $\begin{pmatrix} 600 \\ 400 \end{pmatrix}$ jumps for ever between $\begin{pmatrix} 400 \\ 600 \end{pmatrix}$ and itself. Only $\begin{pmatrix} 500 \\ 500 \end{pmatrix}$ stays fixed, so the fixed vector $\begin{pmatrix} 0.5 \\ 0.5 \end{pmatrix}$ exists all the same.

EXCURSIONCHAINS OF LETTERS

Andrei Markov counts vowels

In 1913 the Russian mathematician Andrei Andreyevich Markov examined the first 20,000 letters of Alexander Pushkin's novel in verse “Eugene Onegin”. He counted how often a vowel was followed by another vowel and how often by a consonant. From this he obtained a $2 \times 2$ transition matrix that described the sequence of letters surprisingly well.

Such models, in which the next state depends only on the present one, are called Markov chains today. Weather forecasts, speech recognition, the ranking of search engines and ecology all work with them, when ecology projects populations into the future as in this chapter.

Source: A. A. Markov: An example of statistical investigation of the text “Eugene Onegin” concerning the connection of samples in chains. Bulletin of the Imperial Academy of Sciences, St Petersburg 1913 · MacTutor: “Andrei Andreyevich Markov”.
